Expectation1: Adhere to site protocols and work effectively as part of the team.
Situation1: A notice has been posted about an optional training session happening next week.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They raise concerns about a policy that seems to disadvantage certain youth, seniors, or refugee applicants.
Story: I wiped the sweat from my brow, glancing at the notice tacked to the breakroom wall: “Optional Training Session—Next Week.” As a construction laborer, I knew the unspoken rule—show up, even if it’s “optional.” The foreman expected us to be team players, to keep up with new safety protocols, to never be the one who falls behind. But as I packed up my gear, my phone buzzed with a message from the advocacy group. They needed me to speak at a council meeting, to challenge a new policy that would make it harder for refugee applicants to access housing. I’d spent weeks gathering stories, promising those affected that I’d be their voice. The meeting was scheduled for the same day as the training. My crew would notice if I skipped; my absence would be a mark against me. But if I didn’t speak up, I’d be letting down people who had no one else. The weight of both worlds pressed on my chest, and I stood there, torn, knowing I couldn’t be in two places at once.
